bp: Micro-videos are built for quick watching and quick sharing. That makes them useful for news, jokes, eyewitness clips, and political messages, but it also makes them a strong carrier for false belief. A short video can mislead without being wholly fake: the scene may be real but reused from another event, the voice or image may be generated by AI, the caption may push a viewer toward a biased interpretation, or several small edits may work together. This paper serves the practical task of debunking such clips in the wild, where a platform, journalist, fact-checker, or safety team needs more than a yes-or-no warning. They need to know what kind of deception is present and what evidence supports that claim. The paper introduces WildFakeBench as a large collection of real micro-videos with expert attribution labels, and FakeAgent as a multi-agent reasoning system that checks video content together with external evidence.
wh: The hard part is that misinformation is not one visual defect. If the problem were only badly edited footage, a detector could search for image artifacts. If it were only false text, it could compare the words to trusted sources. Micro-video misinformation mixes sight, sound, text overlays, captions, generation traces, viewer psychology, and missing context. A real protest clip can be attached to the wrong date. A generated face can be placed beside real news language. A true fact can be framed so that a viewer reaches a false conclusion. Existing benchmarks, according to the abstract, often focus on one deception type, so a model trained on them may learn a narrow habit: spot one kind of trick and miss the others. The second difficulty is explanation. A detector that says fake but cannot say whether the problem is manipulation, AI generation, cognitive bias, or out-of-context reuse is hard to use for debunking.
naive: A smart beginner would collect fake and real videos, train a large vision-language model to label each one, and report the label with a confidence score. That fails because the label hides the reason. The same label fake could mean edited pixels, generated content, misleading framing, or a real clip placed in the wrong story. A second beginner solution would make separate detectors for each known trick. That also breaks in the wild because cases overlap: a video may combine generated material with an out-of-context caption and a bias-inducing narrative. A third shortcut is to trust the video alone. That misses the central fact that context often lives outside the clip, in external evidence about where, when, and why the event occurred.
ap: The central move is to turn fake-video detection into attribution-grounded investigation. The paper first builds WildFakeBench, a benchmark of more than 10,000 real-world micro-videos that covers diverse misinformation types and sources. Each case has expert-defined attribution labels, so the target is not merely true or false but an account of what kind of deception is operating. On top of that data, FakeAgent uses a Delphi-inspired multi-agent reasoning design. The ordinary idea behind this is a structured panel: several checkers examine the same case from different angles, bring in outside evidence, and reason toward a grounded explanation. FakeAgent jointly analyzes what is inside the video and what can be retrieved outside it. Its job is to identify manipulation, recognize cognitive and AI-generated patterns, and detect reuse outside the original context.
mech: The mechanism starts with a micro-video and the information attached to it, such as visible content, possible text or narrative cues, and any signals a multimodal model can read from the clip. Instead of asking for one final label immediately, FakeAgent splits the investigation into reasoning work. One part must understand the video itself: what objects, people, scenes, visual changes, generated-looking patterns, or message cues appear. Another part brings in retrieved evidence, because a clip can only be judged against the world it claims to describe. External evidence may help determine whether the scene belongs to another event, whether the presented claim matches reliable sources, or whether the content pattern resembles known AI-generated or manipulated material. The agents then compare these views rather than letting one dominate. The comparison matters because the clip may look visually plausible while outside evidence contradicts its implied context, or the outside story may sound plausible while the media contains manipulation cues. The system produces attribution-grounded analysis: an explanation that says which misinformation type is implicated and what evidence led there. The benchmark supplies the expert-defined labels needed to train or evaluate this behavior across diverse cases, and the experiments compare FakeAgent against existing multimodal large language models across those misinformation types.
math: The main mathematical idea is evidence aggregation under uncertainty. Each clue is partial. A visual cue may suggest editing, but not prove falsehood. Retrieved evidence may match the topic, but still be incomplete or misleading. A caption may reveal cognitive framing, but the same words could be harmless in another setting. The system therefore needs a way to combine weak signals without pretending any one of them is enough. In everyday terms, aggregation means gathering several imperfect witnesses and asking where they agree, where they conflict, and which claim each witness actually supports. A second idea is classification with attribution: sorting cases into types, while preserving the reason for the sorting. This is different from a plain fake-real score because the output category has to correspond to a human-meaningful cause such as manipulation, AI-generated content, cognitive bias, or out-of-context reuse. A third idea is retrieval-based comparison, which means measuring whether outside evidence is close enough to the video claim to help judge it. The tradeoff is breadth versus false confidence: the benchmark tries to cover many real deception forms, while the reasoning system must avoid turning retrieved or model-generated clues into certainty when the abstract only supports evidence-grounded attribution.
dots: This paper sits inside the repo's misinformation and trust family, whose shared problem is deciding what can be trusted when digital evidence is easy to copy, edit, generate, or detach from its origin. It is close to retrieval-augmented trust work because FakeAgent does not rely only on the item being judged; it brings in external evidence and compares the clip against it. It is also close to multimodal social media safety, because the object is not just text or just image but a compact media package whose meaning comes from several channels at once. In the same batch, PAMAS also uses multiple agents for misinformation detection, but its abstract emphasizes preventing sparse deceptive cues from being drowned by abundant truthful content. FakeAgent instead emphasizes diverse micro-video deception types and attribution labels. Neighboring trust papers such as TrueLens, CiteLLM, and EmeraldApp share the deeper move: fluent or realistic-looking material must be grounded in inspectable evidence.
ww: The approach should work better than a naive detector because it matches the shape of the real failure. Micro-video misinformation is diverse, so a benchmark that includes only one deception type teaches a model an incomplete view of the world. WildFakeBench broadens the training and testing surface by including real cases across multiple misinformation types and sources, with labels that specify why the case is problematic. That makes success depend on recognizing the kind of deception, not only detecting an overall suspicious style. FakeAgent also improves the reasoning path. A single model looking at the video may focus on the most obvious signal and miss context. A structured multi-agent design can separate questions: what does the media show, what outside evidence says, whether the content appears generated or manipulated, and whether the clip is reused outside its original setting. The Delphi inspiration matters as an ordinary design principle: independent or role-separated judgments can reduce one narrow viewpoint dominating the final explanation. The abstract's experimental claim that FakeAgent consistently outperforms existing multimodal large language models across all misinformation types supports this intuition.
po: The payoff is a more useful debunking tool and a more realistic testbed. WildFakeBench gives researchers more than 10,000 real-world micro-videos spanning diverse misinformation types and sources, with expert attribution labels rather than only broad labels. FakeAgent buys the ability to analyze both the video and retrieved evidence, then produce an attribution-grounded account of manipulation, AI-generated patterns, cognitive patterns, or out-of-context misinformation. Grounded in the abstract, the reported result is that FakeAgent consistently outperforms existing multimodal large language models across all misinformation types. For practical users, the important capability is not just flagging a clip, but explaining what went wrong in a way that can support debunking.
limits: The abstract does not prove that the system will keep working against future deception styles, coordinated campaigns, new platforms, or languages outside the data. Expert-defined attribution labels are valuable, but they still depend on the experts' label design and evidence access. Retrieved evidence must be relevant, current, and trustworthy; bad retrieval can give a convincing but wrong explanation. Multi-agent reasoning can expose different angles, but the agents may share the same model weaknesses or repeat errors from the same evidence source. The benchmark has over 10,000 videos, yet real micro-video misinformation is broader than any fixed collection. The abstract reports strong experiments, but not long-term deployment behavior under adversaries who adapt after learning how FakeAgent reasons.
